Should the government decide to turn a portion of the cash into COP, the COP basis would likely rise further . At the same time, corporations may liquidate assets ahead of the April - June tax season to generate COP for tax obligations . Although this liquidation is still months away, it will reduce the flow of local USD buyers while adding to the overall USD inventory, thereby pushing the COP basis higher . records.text: January BoC Preview: Firmly on Hold At its December meeting, the BoC held its policy rate at 2.25% and reiterated that the policy rate was “at about the right level”, assuming the economy evolves in line with its forecasts. This guidance signaled that the BoC was likely to remain on hold at its next several meetings barring significant economic data surprises. Since then, economic data has been mixed, but softer on net. Headline inflation surprised to the upside (largely reflecting seasonal distortions from last year’s VAT holiday) but core inflation surprised to the downside in the December CPI report. Most reassuringly, the three-month annualized average of the BoC’s preferred core measures moderated to 1.7%, consistent with our expectation that fading tariff effects, cooling shelter inflation, and soft wage growth will lower underlying inflation in 2026. In addition, the labor market reversed most of its recent improvement in the December employment report. Job growth softened to 8.2k (vs. 53.6k in November), while the unemployment rate rose by 0.3pp to 6.8%. And while the Q4 BoC surveys suggested some improvement in activity from fading tariff headwinds—consistent with our baseline forecast for a return to trend-like growth in 2026—the spending intentions and the overall business activity indicator remained subdued. records.text: correlation in daily changes between traded inflation and the 2s10s curve for different ranges of inflation, we find that higher inflation steepens the curve when inflation rates are well below target. And as inflation reaches or exceeds the target, higher inflation has a much lower, and even negative correlation with the curve. The patterns observed in the US, EU, and UK all arise from the conventional “DM” market behaviour generated by an inflation targeting central bank. In this situation, volatility in nominal rates exceeds the volatility in medium-term inflation expectations, driven by the embedded inflation-stabilising policy reaction of the central bank priced into markets (Exhibit 8). Policy responses: heading to or from equilibrium? But despite the BoJ raising the possibility of being “behind the curve” on inflation risks, current policy settings in Japan do not seem to be designed to reduce inflation risk and so the JGB curve and the Yen do not exhibit the usual DM correlations. In the context of intervention risk in Yen and JGB markets, it therefore makes sense to analyse the available policy options according to their ability to contain not only market volatility, but also inflation risk. Payback after the spending disruption Accounting for a pickup in BAC card spending growth in the weeks after the storm, we estimate that at least 0.6pp of spending was lost over a one-month period due to Viola. That’s a little more than a quarter of the Jan-Feb swing in total consumer spending. It works out to about a 0.5pp drag on 1Q 2021 GDP growth (on a q/q saar basis). Reasons for a bigger headwind The slowdown in total spending due to Viola might have been larger than the impact on BAC card spending, because cash transactions would most likely have taken a bigger hit. Moreover, some of the rebound in spending growth after Viola might have happened for other reasons. Finally, our estimate above only looks at spending: other components of GDP would also have been affected by Viola. Accounting for these factors, we think the headwind to 1Q 2021 GDP growth from Viola might have been as large as 1.5pp. The analogy isn’t perfect Viola caused significant damage in the South, with extended disruptions to the power grid in Texas. records.text: We wish all of our readers a happy, healthy, and prosperous 2026. In this US n Economics Analyst, we discuss what we think are the most important questions for this year. Our GDP growth forecast is meaningfully above consensus once again this year n (2.5% vs. 2.1% consensus for 2026 Q4/Q4, or 2.9% vs. 2.4% consensus on a full-year basis). The composition of growth is likely to look similar to last year, with business investment again the strongest component of GDP and residential investment again the weakest. We do not see our growth forecast as particularly bold and in fact see some upside risk because we estimate that the combined impact of changes to trade and fiscal policy, changes in financial conditions, and the mechanical effect of the last government shutdown will swing from a 0.5pp drag on 2025 Q4/Q4 growth to a 0.6pp boost to 2026 Q4/Q4 growth. The labor market is now somewhat softer than before the pandemic, and we n expect it to remain in roughly its current balance this year. Slightly firmer final demand growth and a more stable policy environment should support labor demand, though artificial intelligence is likely to cause more noticeable job losses this year in the most exposed areas. The rebalancing of the labor market should keep wage growth at or below its current pace of around 3.5%, a rate that should prove compatible with 2% or lower price inflation at this cycle’s 2% pace of productivity growth. records.text: US Watch | 28 January 2026 3 US Rates US rates were little changed following January FOMC communications. Rates across the curve were within 1-2bps of levels just prior to the communications, there was very modest curve bull flattening, and the mix between real rates & inflation breakevens was little changed. Overall, the rates market took little signal from January FOMC communications. The January FOMC did little to alter our core rate views. Our base case remains relatively range-bound rates for the balance of ’26 & a balance of risks that favors lower, not higher, rates. Our risks assessment is heavily influenced by sentiment reiterated by Powell today: “it is not anybody’s base case right now that the next move will be a rate hike”. If the Fed is unlikely to hike, it is difficult to expect a material increase in front end US rates. We still recommend clients expect lower belly rates, declines in 5Y real rates, & 5s30s steepening. Next week’s Treasury refunding & long end coupon reduction signal risk presents a tactical opportunity to see long end UST outperformance. On policy implementation, there was no change in Fed guidance. The Fed will continue with reserve management purchases (RMPs) at the pace of $40b/m. This pace is expected to continue until mid-April before slowing. We expect RMPs to continue anchoring overnight money markets in the Fed target range & expect to see SOFR set modestly lower in the range & at levels closer to fed funds.

The Fed nonetheless continues to have a downward bias for rates, with Powell and most on the committee still finding current rates as restrictive, although he said it was hard to argue that they were significantly restrictive, as Miran has argued. Given the lack of any policy developments, the first and many subsequent questions during the presser were political in nature. This included Powell attending Lisa Cook’s Supreme Court hearing, his plans after April and any follow-up to his January 11th recorded statement. He of course abstained from providing any additional details, although he did say that Lisa Cook’s hearing was the most important legal event in the Fed’s 113 year history, which combined with his January 11th statement shows that Powell is willing to push back if Fed independence is being severely compromised. This will keep Powell’s ultimate plans after his term as Chair ends in May shrouded until the last minute, particularly given the current DOJ investigation into his role in renovations to the Eccles building. For the moment, Figure 1 shows that policy expectations are still being largely driven by data, which has been resilient into the start of the year. Going with the flow can at times feel complacent; however, any trader knows that fighting momentum can quickly become a painful lesson in the strength of the crowd. The past week has been a powerful reminder that the USD down trend has long legs. We’ve looked for catalysts that might reverse the current—stronger data forcing a less‑dovish Fed, marginal de‑escalation in US foreign policy—only to come up short. As discussed overleaf, although much weakness is already priced in, the headwinds continue to outweigh the tailwinds for the USD. Elsewhere, expectations of policy paralysis persist in the near term as we enter the heart of the next round of central bank meetings. On the short side, although UK data have started to improve, the broader UK economic backdrop remains fragile. Meanwhile, with SNB rates so low, we continue to prefer CHF as a funder. Hedging demand may persist if the KOSPI rally continues but its influence should fade, especially after an 80% KOSPI rally since mid-2025. Implications: First, FX stabilization measures are gaining traction, as evidenced n by falling USD funding premium. Timely and well-coordinated implementation of these measures would significantly support KRW stability. Second, monetary policy alone is unlikely to make meaningful impact on the KRW, given the dominance of equity-related flows not sensitive to rates. Aggressive rate hikes could support the currency but carry high risks of recession and financial instability, which in turn could weaken the KRW. Third, if the KRW remains weak despite solid fundamentals and a benign global backdrop, fiscal policy would have more room to act, supported by higher exporter-driven tax revenues. Finally, recent volatility underscores the importance of close inter-departmental coordination and timely interventions, as daily FX swings can amplify one-sided herd behavior and raise overall market volatility. The Foreign Exchange Holding Indicator (FXHI) measures the extent to which institutional investors are aligned in their currency positioning. It complements State Street's Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI). Because the impact of flows on future retu rns also depends on the positions of institutions in that currency, the FXHI is designed to quantify and measure empirically this aspect of investor behaviour. records.text: sons between China exports data and US import data to selected regions, we could see some re-routing hints: • A material decline in China-US direct trade since the Liberation Day; • A significant increase in China exports to SEA (e.g. Vietnam, Thailand or even India), from which US also experienced significant imports; • A significant increase in China exports to Africa, from which the US has not yet seen significant imports; • A moderate increase in China exports to Europe, from which the US saw stable / slight acceleration in imports; • A decline in China exports to Mexico, from which the US saw no material change in imports as yet. There is no direct evidence that the increased Chinese exports to the SEA countries are all redirected to the US, but the data trends suggest it is likely the case. Europe is probably the region where Chinese players are looking for incremental buyers instead of a re-routing intermediary, while Africa could be at its early stage of establishment as a new hub for Chinese players' supply chains. Besides, Mexico does not appear as a re-routing choice for Chinese players despite the existence of USMCA, and the US also does not see a meaningful increase in imports from Mexico (and even some decline in imports under USMCA). 28 January 2026 6 Barclays | Global Industrials

records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General 3 things only State Street can tell you about investor behaviour Figure 5 USD and EUR Holdings Not for turning The most striking thing about our real money G10 FX flows right now is how unremarkable they are. Only two of the 10 show flows at an extreme (i.e. the top or bottom quintile of their most recent 5 - year history); that is buying of the CHF (flows in the 80th percentile) and selling of the NZD (flows in the 21st percentile). For 5 of the 10, meanwhile, 20-day flows are between the 40th and the 60th percentile, i.e. neutral. With the geo -political backdrop still very uncertain but, at the same time, somewhat r emarkably, FX volatility abnormally low, there seems to be little incentive for longer - term investors to really commit in FX. They have been running an underweight in the USD and overweight in the EUR since late April last year (i.e. just after Liberation Day) and show no strong signs of changing those views anytime soon (albeit we have recently seen some EUR selling). The events of the last week are unlikely to trigger a dramatic rethink of these relatively long-held positions. While we view the JGB curve as too steep, the risk is skewed towards ongoing volatility until the macro picture becomes clearer. Risk premium reduction in Gilts, as the UK’s macro backdrop is improving, remains the main bullish spot in the G4. All in all, we think our macro baseline, coupled with the flows from the Dutch pension reform, suggest the EUR long end, such as 10s30s, will remain steep. Under our baseline, inflation and hike risk remain contained, reducing risks for a flatter curve, while there are multiple paths for further steepening. Core was flat at 3.2%, below consensus of 3.3%, while services rose from 4.4% to 4.5% (0.20%m/m SA), below consensus and BoE's forecast of 4.6%. Upside inflation surprise seals a February hold UK inflation rising more than expected and pick-up in food inflation implies that a back- to-back February cut is very unlikely. And while the labour market continues to soften, in our view, it isn't deteriorating rapidly enough for a back-to-back cut. Inflation pick-up is likely temporary The inflation pick-up is likely temporary as some of the pick-up in December was driven by expected erratic categories (base effects for airfares, rise in tobacco duty). Moreover, core and services inflation surprised on the downside. We expect inflation to edge down to close to 3% in January given base effects from energy and VAT on private schools and fall more decisively from April partly due to Budget measures to reach 2% by H2 2026. This, along with a looser labour market and cooling in pay, keeps the door open for further cuts. We expect cuts in March and June to 3.25%. records.text: FOMC likely on hold for a while The FOMC will almost surely maintain rates at 3.50-3.75%, on January 28. After having cut rates 25bp at each of the last three meetings, the committee signaled at the December meeting it might pause rates at the upcoming meeting if conditions evolved broadly as anticipated, by inserting in its statement a reference to “the extent and timing of additional [rate] adjustments. ” At the same time, the December Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) showed a median dot indicating a single 25bp cut in 2026, to 3.4%, suggesting the FOMC was not eager to cut at the first meeting of the year. Nonetheless, the dot plot made clear that FOMC participants remain very divided about the appropriate rate path with seven of the 19 participants indicating they would not support any cut in 2026, four participants supporting one cut, and the remaining eight favoring two or more cuts. Since then, several FOMC voters have argued that monetary is now well positioned, or in a good place, and have expressed no rush to further lower rates (Figure 14). Labor market conditions have appeared resilient, with the unemployment rate edging down to 4.4% in December and initial claims remaining broadly within historical norms. While payroll employment declined on average by 22k per month in Q4, we attribute most of the decline to government employment reflecting idiosyncratic factors such as DOGE-related retirements. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. Proprietary Indicator Definitions Our proprietary measures of investor behaviour model the flows represented in the aggregated portfolios of sophisticated investors, which account for approximately 15% of the world’s investable securities. The Foreign Exchange Flow Indicator (FXFI) is a measure of the currency flows of institutional investors. It is designed to gauge institutional investor sentiment toward a set of developed and emerging markets currencies. The indicator is derived primarily from longer-dated forward contract flows as these have been shown to be significantly correlated with currency returns. records.text: AI to measure what central banks say . Using Large Language Models (LLM), we analyse policy-relevant remarks in speeches, interviews and press conferences and score them on a hawkish/dovish scale. We show what topics and speakers are driving the shifts in sentiment and provide narrative maps and timelines to illustrate how institutional language evolves. Updated daily, the dataset spans over two decades and is accessible via an interactive dashboard and a Python API ( >Access Dataset ). ECB communication has moved back towards neutral after a dovish phase in Q4. This adjustment is being mostly driven by growth-related language, which remains the marginal swing factor in the ECB's tone, while the inflation tone has been broadly stable since the summer of 2025, closely tracking the underlying data and contributing little to the recent shift in overall sentiment. Evidence from early 2026 is limited but consistent with this picture: Philip Lane has returned to more hawkish language while Luis de Guindos has remained mildly dovish, in line with his historical positioning. See page 2/3 for detail. This report has been prepared by UBS AG London Branch. records.text: Switzerland—2026 Outlook: Moderate Growth, Low Inflation, Stable Rates This year we expect moderate growth, continued low inflation and stable policy rates in Switzerland. The growth picture in particular contrasts with last year, which was characterised by substantial trade distortions. 2025 saw strong growth due to the frontloading of exports ahead of tariffs in Q1, followed by below potential growth in Q2 and a strong contraction in Q3 after the US imposed tariffs of 39% on Swiss exports to the US. That said, activity indicators stabilised in autumn (Exhibit 1, left) and the trade deal reached with the US in November—which caps tariffs at 15%, similar to the EU-US deal—should be a tailwind for growth going forward. In 2025Q4 we expect growth to have picked up to 0.3%qoq, only slightly below potential. This year we expect growth around potential, which we estimate at 1.6% (or 0.4%qoq), as the tariff drag fades and monetary policy remains supportive (Exhibit 2, left). With growth returning towards potential, we expect the unemployment rate to stabilise slightly above its long-run average and the output gap to settle at a slightly negative level, after being positive between 2021 and 2025 (Exhibit 1, right). On an annual basis we expect growth of 1.2% this year—as low growth from 2025H2 pulls down the annual average—slightly above the SNB’s forecast (Exhibit 2, right). See more discussions in our China housing survey takeaways. Data recap: A mixed picture in Q4 growth; 2025 growth target achieved Economic activities concluded 2025 with a mixed picture again. December saw stronger exports (6.6% YoY), service sales and IP growth (5.2% YoY), although retail sales (0.9 YoY) and overall FAI (-16% YoY) weakened further and property downturn continued. In Q4 2025, the official sequential GDP growth accelerated to 4.9% QoQ SAAR from 4.5% in Q3, while a higher base led to a slower YoY pace of 4.5% YoY (vs 4.8% in Q3), in line with market expectation. Overall deflation continued in Q4, although the GDP deflator narrowed to -0.7% YoY (vs -1% in Q3). Growth momentum was mainly underpinned by resilient export growth of 3.9% (vs 6.5% YoY in Q3), which supported solid industrial production (5%, vs 5.8% YoY in Q3). Meanwhile, domestic activities weakened further with continued property downturn, larger decline in both infrastructure and manufacturing FAI, and decelerated retail sales growth. Japan’s Equilibrium Rate Check Since the introduction of Abenomics in 2012, the fiscal and monetary policy mix in Japan has aimed to boost inflation expectations and to keep real rates low. Although it wasn’t the first attempt to reflate Japan, the aggressively reflationary monetary policy over the last 13 years has been the strongest attempt to exit Japan’s liquidity trap and shift to a new inflation equilibrium. Under Governor Ueda, BoJ policy has been to raise rates gradually, but has generally approached tightening delicately given the fragility of inflation in Japan. With the upcoming election seemingly skewing fiscal risks towards further stimulus, there is so far little change in the direction of domestic policy. But with Japanese inflation swaps rising towards 2% (Exhibit 1) and long-end JGB forwards rising to similar levels to other G10 rates markets, volatility in Japanese rates and FX has been rising. In response to this volatility, policymakers in both Japan and the US have signalled willingness to intervene in the market. The key question is whether this rising intervention risk will be used to manage the consequences of the current policy stance, or complement a change in approach from domestic policy. Inflation near 2% — now what? Looking beyond the individual episodes of sharp bond market and currency movements, the rising volatility in Japanese macro assets over recent years is largely a consequence of the rise in Japanese inflation expectations. records.text: 2 US Watch | 28 January 2026 US Economics Statement: a significant hawkish pivot In our view, there were three major hawkish surprises in the January FOMC statement. In the characterization current conditions, the Fed noted that “the unemployment rate has shown some signs of stabilization”. The u-rate declined substantially in December after four consecutive sequential increases. We were surprised by the Fed’s willingness to lean into a single favorable data print. In the assessment of the balance of risks, the committee removed the language saying that it “judges that downside risks to employment rose in recent months.” Instead, it essentially presented risks as balanced. This also seemed like a significant step with private job growth averaging just 29k in the last three months. Last, Governor Bowman did not dissent in favor of a cut, contrary to our expectations. As expected, Governors Waller and Miran did. But interestingly Miran dissented in favor of a 25bp cut, not 50bp. Press conference: validation of market pricing We thought Chair Powell’s tone in the press conference was broadly in line with the statement. Powell’s comments on the labor market mirrored the optimism in the statement. But he also highlighted some pockets of concern, such as the continued drop in the Conference Board’s labor market differential and the rise in part-time employment “for economic reasons”. We expect three factors to raise issuance above consensus in 2026. First, we expect requests for funding of about EUR 135bn (vs EUR 183bn n potential) for the European Recovery Fund (NGEU and RRF). With Member States completing their national plans by the end of August, the EU Commission must conclude programme-related disbursements by the end of December. Second, we expect EU Macro-Financial Assistance to third countries (MFA and n the Ukraine facility) of about EUR 45bn this year and next, driven by the reparation loan to Ukraine approved by the EU Council in December. Third, the EU Commission will provide funding support for defence spending to n 19 Member States via the Security Action for Europe (SAFE). The 2026 disbursements under SAFE will be limited to pre-funding (EUR 22.5bn, 15% of total), and we expect issuance to take place in H2. Last December, the EU targeted a record debt issuance of EUR 160bn for 2026 n (excluding the Ukraine loan). Taking all factors into consideration, we forecast issuance to rise to EUR 170bn, above investors’ expectations, even after accounting for funding frontloading in 2025 and our expectation that EU countries will fall short of full implementation of the Recovery Fund. While Powell said that renewed labor market weakening would clearly call for cutting, both we and the FOMC expect the labor market to remain stable this year. Powell n described the policy stance as “loosely neutral” or “somewhat restrictive” and noted that the December dot plot showed that 15 of 19 FOMC participants anticipate additional normalization. records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Figure 19 Institutional investors are overweight Banks and selling Source: State Street Markets The positive dynamics of trading and banking deals have provided solid performance for a spell, and real money investors have allowed rising share prices to build overweight positions in portfolios. Institutional funds began closing their underweight in Banks in early 2024 and have maintained an overweight throughout 2025. This poses an additional risk to the sector. Other than a bout of buying that we saw in Q2, we have seen nothing but selling since the start of July. This is also quite remarkable, Banks have had decent performance, but long only funds are not willing to see their overweight drift higher than the current levels we’ve seen for a year, taking the opportunity to sell any rally. If they’re selling the upside, and the upside seems to be increasingly at risk, then another potential for a sustained retreat in Banks would be a return to benchmark levels. Even if we don’t see the desire for underweights as we did 2 years ago, the potential for investors to continue to lose faith in the long term sustainability of earnings and more fears on valuations to take hold that a sharp sell off could be in the cards. -10% -5% 0% 5% 10% 15% -0.2% -0.1% 0.0% 0.1% 0.2% 0.3% '22 '22 '23 '24 '25 '26 20d Flows, bps of mkt cap, rh Excess Holdings above Benchmark

records.Author: Goohoon Kwon, CFA; Irene Choi; Danny Suwanapruti; Andrew Tilton
records.text: Rising depreciation pressure in Korea’s FX forward markets suggests a growing influence of KRW hedging demand stemming from the rising value of foreign equity holdings in Korea. KRW forward points—differences between spot and forward exchange rates— have continued to move higher since mid-2025, closely tracking the KOSPI rally over the same period, reflecting USD-buying pressure in forward markets to hedge their increased KRW exposure (Exhibit 4). Taiwan data also show a similar pattern, also reflecting demand for USD forwards to hedge their increased TWD exposure. While hedging new equity purchases is exchange-rate neutral, hedging existing positions increases USD demand in forward markets, pushing up forward points and transmitting depreciation pressure into spot markets. Metals Weekly: Copper fundamentals stumble into the gate as the Year of the Horse draws near Copper prices remain in a high holding pattern as fundamentals have turned even more challenging. A reversal in the front of the COMEX/LME arb has resulted in copper inventory showing up on the LME in the US. Amid LME deliveries in Asia too, the LME copper curve has sharply shifted from backwardation back into contango. In China, weak downstream purchasing has driven pretty aggressive counter-seasonal copper inventory builds. Even with stronger exports over the last months, Chinese copper inventory is still sitting at about 300 kmt at the moment, more than 200 kmt higher than last year at the same time of the inventory cycle (~3 weeks before Chinese New Year). With Chinese New Year approaching on 17 February it will be increasingly difficult to get a “clean” read on Chinese downstream fundamental conditions for the next month and a half. Moreover, with relatively elevated inventory levels already across the base metals, China will likely be heading into the second quarter and peak demand season with a pretty comfortable cushion of buffer stock. While some of the recent acceleration can be pinned to a changing trade balance, there is no denying that the US Economy remains in great shape. Manufacturing is not stellar, but not terrible, personal income and spending remain strong, Industrial production is marching higher, retail sales continues to defy gravity, the anxiety of a housing downturn is proving to be premature as we’re seeing signs of reacceleration in America’s growth engine, the US South (Figure 6) and even the moribund auto industry is seeing some signs of recovery as we polished off 2025. records.Author: Goohoon Kwon, CFA; Irene Choi; Danny Suwanapruti; Andrew Tilton
records.text: Our analysis suggests that the recent KRW decline largely reflects forward market imbalances linked to the KOSPI rally. A sustained surge in Korean equities since mid-2025, combined with policy continuity under the new administration, lifted foreign investors’ Korean equity valuations by 70% to US$950bn at end-2025. Foreign holdings gained further In January by an estimated US$140bn, creating potentially sizable hedging demand even under a single-digit average hedging ratio. (Exhibit 3). In comparison, net foreign inflows to Korea’s stock markets were limited to less than US$1bn for the first three weeks of January. Similar dynamics in forex markets are visible in Taiwan. Foreign holdings of Taiwanese equities rose from 43% of market cap at end-2024 to nearly 50% at end-2025, exceeding US$1.5 trillion (Exhibit 3). With Taiwan equities up 10% YTD, foreign investors likely gained around US$150bn in January, prompting meaningful USD buying in forward markets. The outsized gains in foreign equity holdings contrast with foreign inflows of just US$2.2bn to Taiwan’s stock markets during the first three weeks of January. These TWD hedging flows from equity investors, together with regulatory relaxation of USD hedging requirements for Taiwan life insurers, appear to have contributed to TWD weakness despite Taiwan’s record current account surplus of 20% of GDP in Q3, driven by the AI boom. PCE uses Producer Price Index (PPI) health insurance data as an input, and Medicare Advantage coverage is primarily categorized under PPI’s “individual comprehensive medical service plans.” This category typically resets every January to reflect new Medicare Advantage payment rates. records.text: M Update 2 January FOMC: A dovish hold In justifying the decision to stay on hold in January, Chair Powell pointed to incoming economic data, which was stronger than expected, “some signs” of stabilization in the labor market, and continued confidence that tariff-induced inflation would be transitory. He said that downside risk to employment had likely diminished — which was the original reasoning behind the risk-management rate cuts — but also said upside risk to inflation had declined. The broad consensus at this meeting was to remain on hold and most FOMC members see the current policy stance as appropriate to stabilize the labor market and guide inflation lower. We interpret Powell’s comments as indicating the Fed still has an easing bias and, as a result, just executed a “dovish hold.” He said that the current funds rate target was at the upper end of the plausible range of estimates for neutral and that the policy rate was appropriately set to help guide inflation lower. On net, that suggests the Fed still sees the monetary policy stance as imparting some restriction or at the very least not boosting the economy. He was noncommittal about whether further cuts would come because of labor market softness or inflation moving lower, but the Fed’s forecast and our interpretation of the press conference is that the Committee likely expects to reduce policy rates only after it sees evidence that inflation is decelerating. records.text: January FOMC Recap: Some Signs of Stabilization The main message from the January FOMC meeting was that better growth news and early signs of labor market stabilization left the Committee feeling well-positioned—a term Chair Powell used five times—to remain on hold today while they assess the incoming data. The FOMC noted in its statement that the unemployment rate has shown “some signs of stabilization” and removed an earlier reference to downside risks to employment having risen. During the press conference, Powell similarly noted that data since the last meeting showed a “clear improvement in the outlook for growth” and “evidence of stabilization” in the labor market. Powell qualified this by making it clear that he does not see the evidence of stabilization as definitive just yet, which is our view as well. He echoed the language in the statement that there have been “some signs of stabilization,” but added that he “wouldn’t go too far with that” and that there are also “some signs of continued cooling,” such as the latest decline in the Conference Board’s measure of job availability. Both we and the FOMC expect the labor market to remain stable this year, with the unemployment rate moving roughly sideways in the mid-4s. This could prove wrong, in which case, Powell said, “clearly a weakening labor market calls for cutting.” But if it proves right, then the next cut will probably not come for a while. records.text: Potential Pipeline Constraints - Eyes on labor availability and latest anecdotes The US power industry is poised to require >500,000 new workers by 2030 or a significant acceleration in labor productivity. This growth enters a labor force already facing strain from aging and a limited pipeline of skilled labor. Labor demand challenges to meet levels of US power demand growth not seen since the 1990s are rising amid the Demographic Dilemma — a shrinking productive labor pool tasked to support an aging population — which raises the risk of G7 labor force strains. This is elevating investor/corporate debates on industry execution and whether/when rising power, equipment and labor costs could constrain growth. Generational Growth to achieve 2.6% CAGRs in electricity demand through 2030 could require ~510K US power and grid jobs (28% growth vs. the 2023 US energy workforce). We estimate the need for ~300K incremental jobs across manufacturing, construction and operations/maintenance (Exhibit 9), plus an additional 207K across US transmission and distribution (Exhibit 10). For US rates, potential for fewer cuts, wider budget deficits, strong productivity gains, large hyperscaler debt issuance, and fiscal developments in Japan and Germany all suggest that the balance of risks points toward still higher long-end yields. We have a much higher-than-consensus 10y yield forecast of 4.50% for end-2026. However, there is one major risk to our view. T he administration appears to want reduced back-end yields to address affordability concerns going into the midterm elections. We think the most potent, logical and practical pathway is by lowering long-term Treasury supply via cutting auction sizes. This is a risk we have discussed since April 2025. We estimate the Fed alone could absorb approximately two-thirds of net T-bill supply this year. That gives the Treasury room to consider adjusting its supply from long -end bonds to issuing more bills for the private market. On each given day, we blend data by adding the total quoted amount in the order book from both sources for each displayed currency pair. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. For example, a 90th percentile reading for EURUSD indicates that the current depth of book value is ranked in the top 10% of historical observations over the last year. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Over the weekend after the 23 January BoJ policy meeting, the JPY appreciated a sharp 3%, reportedly “triggered by indicative preparation for intervention by US”, taken as a strong overseas’ pressure to accelerate a BoJ policy rate hike. While we think that the BoJ could indeed hike in April and make up its “behind-the-curve” reputation, we think that the current change is too fast and close our paid April OIS which we entered on 14 January. With the market’s perception changing for a faster BoJ hike or hikes, the IRS curve up to the 5y flattened sharply, taking 1y2y-3y2y back to December 2025 levels (Figure 2). It was even twist-flattening, as 1y2y rose 1bp and 3y2y fell by 8bp compared with about a week ago. records.text: We don't expect the statement to provide specific guidance about the future course of policy, but we think it will suggest patience. The statement will likely reiterate that "In considering the extent and timing of additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. " This would indicate that the FOMC is in no rush to further adjust rates down toward what the median participant sees as the neutral rate in the longer-run. Regarding the balance sheet, we expect the statement to state that the committee will continue purchasing shorter-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain an ample supply of reserves on an ongoing basis. One dissent likely We expect Governor Miran to dissent again in favor of a 50bp cut at this meeting, as he has done at each of the meetings since he joined the FOMC, in September. Miran has been explicit that he views the stance of monetary policy as restrictive and that it should be eased significantly. At the other end of the spectrum, while incoming voters Hammack and Logan have expressed concerns about recent rate reductions, our baseline is that they would not dissent against holding rates unchanged at this meeting. That said, we would not be totally surprised if a Fed president expressed a preference for a rate hike. Meanwhile, income fundamentals seemed less supportive than prior data suggested. Weaker- than-anticipated income in October and November and continued spending led the personal saving rate to decline to 3.5% in November (Figure 5), well below the 6.4-8.5% that prevailed during 2019. We interpret this low saving rate with caution, as the shortfall between income and spending is likely to reflect, at least in part, measurement issues. Labor market indicators point to solid conditions at the end of 2025. December saw a nonfarm payroll gain of 50k after prints in October and November that were affected by idiosyncratic developments in the government sector (Figure 6). records.text: Canada retaliated against US tariffs by imposing tariffs on C$96bn of US imports in March and April, thereby raising the effective tariff rate on Canadian imports by 3pp.1 Canada removed most of these tariffs (but kept tariffs on steel, aluminium and autos) in September—thereby lowering the increase in the Canadian effective tariff rate to 1pp— in an effort to restart USMCA negotiations. Given the abrupt removal of its counter-tariffs, we see Canada as a potentially useful case study for how firms might respond if US tariffs are removed (which we expect would lead to a similar 2pp decline in the US effective tariff rate after tariffs are reimplemented). In Exhibit 1, we compare the price trend for consumer goods exposed to tariffs from March-September with the trend for unaffected categories. Inflation for tariffed goods increased sharply in March and remained elevated while tariffs were in place. Following the removal of tariffs in September, inflation on tariffed categories undershot other non-energy goods. To more rigorously assess how prices responded to the removal of counter-tariffs, we leverage a panel of food price data to statistically detect the impact of both tariff implementation and removal. The advantages of using food prices are twofold. First, data on consumer prices for food are more detailed than for other consumption categories, allowing for a cleaner partition of tariffed and non-tariffed goods. In such a scenario, if the RBA eventually chooses not deliver a hike in February, rate hike pricing for February should shift to the next two meetings. With how little it is priced in March RBA versus May RBA, we think the Feb/Mar spread stands out as the most to gain, especially if markets start to view the RBA as behind the curve. As such, we are rotating our position in front-end AUD rates, shifting from a paid position in Feb/May RBA to Feb/Mar RBA. Although both positions will move in the same direction depending on Q4 CPI, restructuring it this way allows us to lock in some of our existing gains, while also improving the risk-reward profile of our trade. See more discussions in our China housing survey takeaways. Data recap: A mixed picture in Q4 growth; 2025 growth target achieved Economic activities concluded 2025 with a mixed picture again. December saw stronger exports (6.6% YoY), service sales and IP growth (5.2% YoY), although retail sales (0.9 YoY) and overall FAI (-16% YoY) weakened further and property downturn continued. In Q4 2025, the official sequential GDP growth accelerated to 4.9% QoQ SAAR from 4.5% in Q3, while a higher base led to a slower YoY pace of 4.5% YoY (vs 4.8% in Q3), in line with market expectation. Overall deflation continued in Q4, although the GDP deflator narrowed to -0.7% YoY (vs -1% in Q3). Growth momentum was mainly underpinned by resilient export growth of 3.9% (vs 6.5% YoY in Q3), which supported solid industrial production (5%, vs 5.8% YoY in Q3). Meanwhile, domestic activities weakened further with continued property downturn, larger decline in both infrastructure and manufacturing FAI, and decelerated retail sales growth. Value-added growth of service sectors stayed robust at 5.2% (vs 5.4% YoY in Q3). Full year GDP growth printed 5%, achieving government’s growth target. See more in our Dec & Q4 data comment. The most recent bout of USD weakness confirms the broader downtrend, and the magnitude of the move does not imply that the worst is fully priced. While the latest leg lower was catalysed by a strengthening JPY, several additional factors beyond the JPY are contributing to sustained USD weakness. Notably, this move is not being driven by traditional influences, as the DXY has decoupled from both growth indices and rates markets. Although such divergences are typically unsustainable, the breadth of current drivers suggests this move could persist. The first atypical driver is gold. Gold and the USD remain inversely correlated, and the gold rally can persist. With nominal growth expectations rising for 2026, a common question we receive from investors is whether a potential return of inflation and associated increase in nominal yields could serve as a headwind for valuation this year. Our work actually shows that over extended periods, equities tend to see strong returns in rising nominal yield environments as long as growth is improving. In fact, the strongest bond yield/ISM backdrop for the equal weighted S&P 500 is yields up/ISM up (20% annualized return). Returns are also strong in a yields down/ISM up environment (14% annualized return), which is more in line with our house view on the rates side for 2026. The reason for these dynamics is that inflation is positively correlated to revenues over time. The added piece is that US equity indices are goods heavy, which is where the pricing power is likely to be in '26, in our view. records.text: GLOBAL RESEARCH Shutdown to have lingering effects on the inflation data The December CPI data brought a slightly cleaner read of inflation than the November report, but there was still plenty of noise. Specifically, we saw the relatively firm prints for food, housing furnishings, apparel, medical care commodities & services, lodging away from home, and airfares as payback for a soft November. The good news is that sequential inflation prints for these categories should be more signal than noise over the coming months notwithstanding the annual January effect. The bad news is that distortions will remain a feature of the inflation data for some time, especially when it comes to the y/y data. That is largely because of the BLS’ use of carry-forward imputation to estimate rents and owner equivalent rent inflation in November. Since the rent data are collected using six panels of the housing survey, each of which are surveyed once every six months, the data will not show payback in rent and OER inflation until April. That means, that the y/y rate will be biased lower until April and then be biased higher from October 2026 to March 2027 because of base effects. Bumpy YoY inflation path = large monthly roll swings As a result of the distortions in YoY rate from shutdown impacts, the market is pricing large swings in YoY inflation. records.text: Setting a New Record With Upside Risk This year is likely to be a record year for EU debt issuance. The EU funding plan presented last December set a target of EUR 160bn, excluding the reparation loan to Ukraine. Taking all factors into consideration, and in light of the roughly EUR30bn of funding already raised in 2025, we forecast that EU net debt issuance will fund about EUR130bn (vs EUR 183bn potential) of Recovery Fund disbursements, EUR 45bn of the Ukraine loan, and about EUR20bn of SAFE, for a total of about EUR170bn, above investors’ expectations. But complete implementation of the European Recovery Fund and SAFE could push EU debt issuance even higher, by about EUR50bn, to a record level of EUR220bn this year (Exhibit 5). In 2026, it will be key for market participants to monitor the implementation of the European Recovery Fund as the main source of upside risk to EU debt issuance. records.text: of data after tariffs were removed, the inflation rate for the tariffed group normalized back to only slightly below the control group’s trend. These patterns suggest that implementing tariffs boosted prices, but removing them did not lead to meaningful price declines, at least in the short term. These results are consistent with findings in the academic literature of “downward nominal price rigidity.” Analysis of the 2018-19 trade war found that consumers bore the brunt of tariff increases, with passthrough estimates averaging around 70%. While evidence on the price effects of tariff removal is more limited, episodes of tariff liberalization in EMs point to muted downward price effects.2 A more extensive literature on the effects of sales tax reform points to a similar asymmetry between the effect of tax increases and declines on firms’ pricing decisions.3 This asymmetry was also highlighted in the BoC’s Business and Consumer surveys in Q4. Near-term inflation expectations (as reported in the BoC’s surveys) were little changed among both firms and consumers after counter-tariffs were removed. Furthermore, the BoC’s writeup flagged one respondent’s expectation that “I’ve never seen prices go down. With the tariffs gone, companies will stop raising prices and leave it at what it is.” In addition to price dynamics, we also examine the impact of tariff removal on import flows in Exhibit 3. The current elevated terms of trade are incompatible with the prevailing low levels of belly rates, in our eyes. Historically, strong terms of trade have coincided with high belly rates as the market discounted higher future growth and tighter monetary policy. But assuming underlying inflationary pressure remains buoyant in Japan, the market reaction and correlation patterns will depend on the policy choices from this list. The options are not mutually exclusive and indeed are likely to be combined, and can be implemented by degree. The standard policy response to reduce upside risks to inflation would be to raise policy rates sufficiently to tighten financial conditions, or tightening fiscal policy. Both have the effect of reducing growth expectations, either via tighter financial conditions or directly via weaker (government) demand. Intervention in either Yen or JGBs could reduce volatility in the asset directly affected, but in the absence of other policy shifts run the risk of transmitting volatility elsewhere or having only a temporary effect. Two-sided intervention risk is potentially more powerful, in that significant resolve to adjust the level of USDJPY could be more credible and ultimately have some effect on inflation. But such a two-sided commitment would likely require additional policy commitments from Japan to reduce volatility from inflation. records.text: Inflation Strategist | 28 January 2026 7 Don’t fade the beta bounce This is a classic ‘beta breakeven’ trade – being both long on a real yield basis and long breakevens (or in this case, using inflation swaps, we show it as twice the inflation rate less the nominal rate). And the macro inconsistency provides the intuitive logic for considering it. The beta bounce we’ve seen since year-end, with both a softening in €str rates and firmer breakevens/inflation rates, is both annoying and reassuring. Annoying because we’re now considering ‘buying the beta’ at higher levels than prevailed a couple of weeks ago, and reassuring because the sharp fall into year-end has been arrested. But which beta? Exhibit 8 suggests the period between the 1y and 5y horizons is perhaps most interesting – when €str is priced to rise despite inflation being well below target. And this 1y4y span is also appealing from a roll-down perspective. 4y €str is priced to rise by 19bp over the next twelve months (from 2.21% to 2.40%) but 4y inflation is priced to rise only 4bp (from 1.88% to 192%). So the lion’s share of the implied rise in the nominal rate over a year is in the real rate, and this means that the 1y4y ‘beta breakeven’, at 143bp, is 12bp lower than the spot 4y beta breakeven at 155bp (i.e., 12bp of roll-down over twelve months, Exhibit 12). records.text: Carlin Doyle 26 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Turkey – Still Got It As far as EM carry trades go, the TRY is hard to beat in terms of risk/return. Even with interest rates far lower then their peak and a course of steady nominal currency depreciation, the lira carry trade is better than any other EM currency – even compared to some of the exotics. Moreover, FX positioning is light and the upward revision to the outlook on Turkish FX debt by Fitch on Friday marks a seal of approval. How the country manages if economic growth slows rapidly is a different question. So far, recession has been avoided, which has kept President Erdoǧan quiet. Long may that continue. Turkish central bank (TCMB) governor Fatih Karahan likes to keep markets guessing. The latest monetary policy announcement on 22 January saw the key interest rate lowered by 100 bps, compared to 150bps expected. In December the bank cut by more than forecast. No easy policy options Recent policy actions highlight the tensions between the current policy framework and revealed policymaker preferences, as well as the possible route to a smooth transition. At the current juncture, US officials have expressed concern over volatility in the JGB market, and BoJ officials have suggested they could make adjustments to their bond purchases to dampen volatility in the long end. At the same time, Japanese officials have commented that they are uncomfortable with the weak Yen, and it is weighing on public sentiment, and US officials have reportedly stepped in to try to strengthen JPY. This can work for a time, but reducing volatility in both rates and FX without a change in the underlying policy mix or macro backdrop is a challenging task. As a result, until the BoJ moves towards more expeditious hikes or fiscal policy becomes more restrained, intervention alone is unlikely to deliver a lasting stabilisation of inflation risk, nor convince the market of a shift in reaction function from the BoJ at higher levels of inflation. records.text: 016) find that copper price shocks continue to affect mining investment significantly, especially when these shocks are large and persistent. In cases of greater persistence, mining investment tends to rise by over 1pp of GDP; in contrast, a transitory shock typically boosts this investment by less than 0.4pp of GDP. Better prospects for mining investment are already showing up in the data. According to national copper agency Cochilco, mining investment rose around 10% last year from 2024, and average investment projected for 2026–27 stands 14% above the previous estimate. A study by the BCCh suggests that an increase in mining investment of this magnitude can lift GDP growth by 0.3- 0.4pp, with two-thirds stemming from higher construction activity. Elevated copper production should also add to growth, we think. According to BCCh estimates (see December 2023 IPoM) using the input-output matrix, a 1% increase in mining production raises GDP growth by 0.18pp, with around 80% of the effect being direct and the remainder reflecting indirect spillovers to business services, industry and commerce. With copper production growth expected to accelerate from around 2% last year to 3.7% in 2026 and about 6.4% next year, mining output could add around 0.3pp to growth in 2026 relative to last year, and up to 0.5pp next year. Although the economy continues to hum, inflation expectations are rising and expectations of Fed cuts continue to be delayed, USD weakness persists. The relationship between the USD and traditional fundamentals—economic strength and rates —has become exceptionally weak in recent weeks. This suggests that it’s not conventional economics driving the move (apologies to the Fed‑watchers); instead, the more influential drivers right now are gold and investor sentiment. How far can Gold run? Several forces could be at play regarding the Gold/USD relationship—USD debasement concerns, a desire to diversify across safe-haven assets. T here is still room for gold holdings to grow. Both retail investors and central banks theoretically have capacity to add exposure. Retail investors appear overweight relative to history, but positioning was technically higher in 2020. records.text: M Idea 2 2027 advance MA rate notice: inflationary implications The Center for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced that capitation payments to private insurance companies—those administering Medicare Advantage plans—would rise by only 0.09% from 2026 to 2027. This near zero increase fell sharply below insurer expectations, as the industry had broadly anticipated a more typical 3-5% rise in payments. The unexpectedly flat update immediately complicated the revenue outlook for Medicare Advantage insurers, who now face the prospect of operating in 2027 with payment growth that does not keep pace with medical costs. Our equity analysts think that it is less likely to see a significant upward revision between the Advance Notice and the Final Rate Announcement like what occurred last year (see here). We received many questions from clients on the potential implications for US inflation. Because Medicare Advantage plays a large role in the structure of U.S. health care payments, it is natural to ask whether an unexpected slowdown in government payments to insurers could meaningfully alter the path of health insurance inflation. Our assessment is that the disinflationary effects are modest and delayed for CPI. To understand this connection, it is important to recall the basic structure of Medicare Advantage. As Medicare Part C, it is a form of Medicare coverage administered by private insurance companies rather than by the government’s traditional fee for service program. Pr

records.text: EUR Curve Steep But Stable Throughout 2025, the back end of the EUR curve steepened, with 10s30s steepeners among the most profitable, vol-adjusted curve trades in European and global rates. This was in part driven by anticipation of the Dutch pension reform, with funds generally eligible to make the transition from defined benefits (DB) to defined contributions (DC) from the beginning of 2026. This transition implies a decrease in hedging demand for longer-dated liabilities, and reduced holdings of duration vs equities and other real assets. By benchmarking against the reduction in DB liabilities, we argued the Dutch pension reform was worth 20-30bp of curve steepening in 10s30s. But although the EUR curve steepened notably last year, it was not an outlier among peers (Exhibit 1). In fact, we would argue the European curve steepening is part of a broader shift in the balance between supply and demand for duration. On the former, elevated or rising deficits and central bank QT have pushed higher government bond free-floats. On the latter, a reassessment of inflation risk in some jurisdictions drove higher rates, which in turn reduced liabilities in the pension and insurance sector. Combined with shifts in the mix of retirement savings, this structurally reduced demand for long-end bonds. Against this, we have estimated that up to half of the total steepening in 10s30s might have been due to foreign spillovers. Since then, supply adaptation by issuers such as the UK and Japan,

records.text: The Reparation Loan to Ukraine Brings Macroeconomic Financial Assistance to a Different Level Before the Invasion of Ukraine, the Macroeconomic Financial Assistance (MFA) that the EU provided to neighbouring countries of strategic interest was limited to a few billions of Euros at best., Since 2022, financial assistance to third countries (MFA and Ukraine facility) has steeply increased to an annual rate of about EUR 20bn because of the support to Ukraine. EU financial assistance will jump up by about EUR 45bn in both 2026 and 2027 because of the reparation loan to Ukraine that the EU Council approved in December. Notably, the loan was approved after the EU Commission presented its 2026 funding plan at EUR 160bn and it is therefore reasonable to assume that the related annual disbursement should be treated as entirely additional. Legislative proposals are now in place at the EU Parliament and Council, with the European Commission providing financial support to Ukraine from the second quarter of 2026. The approval process is on track and we expect the EU Commission to move forward with the adoption of the relevant Implementing Decisions so that it can make its first disbursement of the loan as soon as April (Exhibit 3). November monthly activity data picked up (0.8%M) after disappointing October (-0.2%Q), which was however also revised upwards. While the monthly indicators remain volatile, we expect the 4Q data to confirm the recovery momentum in Sweden. Household consumption, running at 3.3%Y in November, should be one of the main positive drivers. We also expect net trade and investments to contribute to the upside. Looking at the industry composition however, we expect services to be supportive (also in line with the surveys), while industrial production has likely contracted on a quarterly basis (as shown by a decline in orders). Strong outlook, but risks remain: We remain positive on the Swedish growth outlook, given the encouraging hard data described above, the significant improvements in the surveys and the fiscal spending coming this year. However, risks remain. One of the main domestic risks for the growth outlook remains the willingness of households to spend rather than save. The 4Q data so far confirms that the trend is up in household spending and we think the momentum to spend can sustain into 2026, especially as the food VAT reduction will come in April. This more constructive outlook reflects better terms of trade, an expected recovery in credit and the construction industry, and improved business and consumer sentiment. We still anticipate the BCCh keeping rates on hold in 2026, although more dovish signaling has introduced downside risks to this view. The policy statement leaned a bit hawkish in our view, with the state of the economy upgraded to solid, the jobs market stabilizing, while risks to the dual mandate is again balanced. Additionally, we note that Miran’s dissent in favor of cutting by 25 bps is a moderation from the 50bps of cuts he voted at each meeting since he joined the FOMC. Waller also dissented, while the remaining voting members agreed with the policy hold, including the newly rotated generally hawkish regional presidents. In all fairness, the lack of substantive changes, most of which had been widely anticipated, made for an unilluminating press conference. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

This view is not based on concerns about inflation. Instead, it reflects upside risks to growth and doubts about the need for additional impulse from monetary policy when the real policy rate stands close to neutral territory amid elevated global uncertainty. Inflation is likely to remain below 3% in H1, helped by CLP appreciation, weak tradable goods prices and disinflationary pressures from imported goods (including from China). We expect inflation to reaccelerate during H2 and end the year slightly above 3% (Figure 7). Despite our call for stable rates through 2026, recent signals from the BCCh introduced some downside risks to this view. If they materialize, the discussion could shift toward higher rates in 2027. First, the December IPoM policy corridor embeds a rate cut around mid-2026. More recently, at the 27 January policy meeting, the central bank noted that near-term inflation could come in below its baseline scenario and said it would assess the implications in the March IPoM. This opened the door for a rate cut earlier than envisaged in December, giving the meeting statement a dovish tone. On an annual basis we see growth at 1.2% this year, slightly above the SNB’s forecast, and 1.6% next year. Inflation has stabilised slightly above 0%, and we expect it to remain subdued n but positive throughout this year. Towards the end of this year and into 2027 we expect headline inflation to move up towards 0.6%, in line with the SNB’s forecast. This inflation outlook is supported by our FX strategists’ expectation of a slight depreciation of the Swiss Franc against the Euro. That said, we see risks to the inflation outlook tilted towards the downside if the Franc remains stronger than we expect and if labour market weakness weighs more strongly on domestic inflation. Against this backdrop of moderate growth, we expect the SNB to remain on hold n at 0% for the foreseeable future. records.text: The pace and sourcing of US power infrastructure is a front and center area of focus for investors given implications for the pace of AI deployment as a driver of our 2.6% CAGR in US power demand through 2030. In this note, we analyze the generation capacity data from the EIA to keep track of currently planned and added capacity. We believe Parts/People availability are among the key drivers/constraints to AI/data center (and broader) power demand growth, and the latest EIA data is supportive for renewables development through 2030 amid policy incentives sunsetting. We highlight NextEra (NEE, Buy) as the stock most leveraged to the renewables theme in our Utilities coverage, as it currently operates the largest portfolio of renewables in the US and plans to double its size by the end of 2027, and also plans to add 4-8 GW of natural gas power plants in 2030-2032. We provide further detail regarding net generation capacity additions by technology, planned capacity projects development stages, cumulative delays, cancellations/postponement and expected capacity additions in 2026-2030. Our main takeaways are: Net generation capacity additions totaled ~50GW in 2025, representing 80% of our n estimates for 2025. Notably, ~1.3 GW of CCGT capacity got added in December, and CCGT capacity adds surpassed our estimates for the year, totaling 1.8 GW vs our 1.1 GW. Will net job losses in the most AI-exposed industries increase meaningfully? Yes. We see the labor market as the most uncertain piece of the 2026 economic outlook, and the most difficult question about the labor market is, To what degree will companies replace workers with artificial intelligence or at least hold off on hiring? Artificial intelligence has played only a small role in the slowdown in job growth so far, accounting for net job losses of about 5-10k in the subindustries shown in Exhibit 8 where the technology is most ready to deploy. But we think that AI has the potential to eventually automate a large share of job tasks and displace 6-7% of current jobs. AI adoption increased last year, especially in areas where work tasks are more exposed to AI automation, and many companies appear eager to implement AI to reduce labor costs. As a result, we expect to see a more meaningful decline in employment in these industries of at least 20k per month in 2026, though this should be partly offset by AI-related job gains in other areas. With respect to economic fundamentals, although Powell will likely continue to emphasize that downside risks remain prominent for the labor market, his tone may sound somewhat more sanguine. Better productivity could imply that potential growth is higher than currently estimated and therefore the output gap is less positive than assumed. In this context, estimates from the latest National Productivity Report pointing to productivity gains of 0.5% in 2026 raise the possibility of a reassessment of the output gap in the March IPoM that could bring forward the rate cut currently penciled in for mid-2026. Our base case remains that improving growth prospects will eventually discourage the need for additional easing. Alternatively, if a rate cut does materialize, we would see a higher probability of rate hikes next year, as stronger activity could increase medium-term inflationary pressures. records.text: 9. Will the effective tariff rate rise meaningfully further? No. With the midterm elections less than a year away, polls suggest that the cost of living continues to be the top issue of concern to voters. We think this will deter the White House from raising tariff rates further this year. In fact, we think the effective tariff rate is likely to fall slightly, for two reasons. First, new deals or exemptions could modestly dilute some current tariffs. Second, the Supreme Court looks more likely than not to rule that some of the tariffs the administration has imposed so far are illegal. While the White House would likely seek to reimpose tariffs under different authorities if the court blocks the IEEPA tariffs, the risks nevertheless lean toward lower tariff rates, as an across-the-board replacement under Section 122 would be capped at 15%—some administration officials have suggested it might be imposed at 10%—while country-specific rates under Section 301 would require investigations that could be impractical to conduct for all trading partners and, in any case, would likely take time to complete following a Supreme Court ruling. 10. Will there be any major new fiscal stimulus measures ahead of the midterm elections? records.text: Recent KRW Performance: The Korean Won weakened again in January, n reversing part of its sharp rebound in late December. This occurred despite strong KOSPI gains. Given heightened FX volatility, the Bank of Korea shifted its guidance from easing to neutral despite a negative output gap and a recent softening in activity. Key KRW drivers: Forward-market pressures appear to be the main source of n KRW weakness. Equity outflows from local retail and foreign investors fell by half in January compared with Q4, but the KOSPI rally boosted the value of foreign equity holdings by US$140bn, creating potentially sizable hedging demand even under a single-digit average hedging ratio. Rate differentials: The rate gaps between the US and Korea have narrowed after n three Fed cuts since mid-2025, suggesting that US-Korea rate gaps were not the key driver for the recent KRW weakness. More broadly, positive spot-forward correlations for the KRW since mid-2023 point to the increasing role of non-rate factors in Korea’s forex markets, similar to trends seen in Taiwan, where large foreign stock holdings of over US$1.5 trillion have long influenced FX dynamics. The KRW outlook: We continue to expect the KRW to appreciate over the next n 12 months to below 1400 per USD, supported by recent stabilization measures, foreign inflows tied to KTB inclusion in the WGBI, and improvement in the current account. records.text: Analytics, Barclays Research January FOMC statement to signal continued pause We expect the FOMC statement to mention that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace, in light of the strong activity data for Q3, and solid gains in consumer spending in October and November. Regarding the labor market, we expect the statement to note that over the past year, job gains have slowed and the unemployment rate has edged up. We also expect it to mention that inflation has moved up in recent months and remains elevated. We don't think the FOMC would take much signal from the relatively muted core PCE prints in October and November, given that they were likely affected by shutdown-related distortions. We think the statement will reiterate that the committee is attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate, but that it will no longer highlight downside risks to employment, suggesting that it views downside risks to employment and upside risks to inflation as more balanced. 26 January 2026 3 Barclays | Federal Reserve Commentary

records.text: Megan Peters +44(20)7051-2058 | megan.l.peters@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Global Economics Comment: What Happens When Tariffs Go Away? A Lesson from Canada 25 January 2026 | 10:38PM GMT Tariffs lifted US inflation in 2025 as higher costs passed through to consumer n prices. But tariffs on some countries or goods might be reduced or eliminated (at least in the near-term) if the US Supreme Court rules against President Trump’s IEEPA authority in the coming weeks. In this Global Economics Comment, we leverage the recent experience in Canada—where retaliatory tariffs implemented in March/April were removed in September—to shed insight on what happens to prices and trade flows when tariffs go away. Inflation on tariffed goods increased sharply following tariff implementation and n has softened since tariffs were removed. That said, statistical analysis shows that the inflation slowdown since September reflects a return to trend rather than outright price declines. This pattern is consistent with findings in academic studies that find that tariff implementation and removal have asymmetric price impacts. Canada’s imports from the US partially rebounded after Canada removed its n counter-tariffs, with import volumes recovering about half of their decline within two months. records.text: ab 26 January 2026 Global Research US Economic Data Another healthy core orders report Core orders rise 0.7% in November Durable goods orders rose 5.3% in November, versus the 2.7% we expected and the 3.8% expected by consensus, with orders of nondefense aircraft and parts rising 97.6% over the month. Could "animal spirits" and a better growth outlook nurture a deal pipeline? Yes – especially given that real estate markets are stabilizing. Most direct lending will have a real estate or physical asset nexus, in our view. For example, consider the monetization of non-core assets. Hospitals, universities, and governments own significant amounts of real estate, much of which could be monetized while preserving core functions. We think several trends are aligning that would favor more of these loans coming to fruition: • Less "free money" – stimulus is harder to come by: Most stimulus money has been spent, leaving fewer options for nonprofits and governments seeking to raise liquidity. • Rising expenses: Soaring construction costs and elevated personnel expenses make outsourcing capex, whether through a leaseback or a P3, operationally attractive. • A good growth outlook: A loan is still debt, and municipal borrowers typically only borrow when they have confidence in the future. A stronger growth outlook gives governments and nonprofits the confidence to implement their capital plans.

records.text: Evidence From Market Data on the Role of Interest Rate Differentials Another potentially important driver of the recent KRW depreciation could be US–Korea rate differentials. However, the policy rate gap between the US and Korea has narrowed following three Fed cuts, suggesting that these rate differentials were not the main driver of the recent KRW weakness. This narrowing has occurred in both actual and expected rates since mid‑2025 (Exhibit 5). Similarly, the Fed’s rate cuts have also reduced policy rate differentials between the US and Taiwan. Along with narrowing rate differentials, forex hedging demand typically declines, although both can also move in the same direction. While rate differentials matter for hedging decisions in principle, other factors have become increasingly influential in recent years. With policy uncertainty rising—particularly around tariffs and geopolitical risks—investors may boost forex hedging for risk management rather than strictly for hedging costs or returns. In this context, the USD funding premium—another component of hedging costs—can influence hedging decisions as much as rate gaps, especially in volatile markets, as seen in late 2022 in Korea when market rates spiked amid money‑market stress. The growing importance of non‑rate factors in Korea’s forex markets is also reflected in the positive flips in spot–forward correlations for the KRW since mid‑2023. Having spent the past 2 weeks in Japan, it’s clear that the country is on a much different path than it has been for the past 30 years. First, deflation is a distant memory. In fact, most people (wealthy, middle and lower income) are now feeling the impact of inflation, and it’s not just goods prices. It’s rents, food, travel, leisure, fuel and utilities. From an American consumer perspective, the perception of price points is totally different because of the weak yen. Skiers will appreciate that a daily lift ticket at the major resorts is around $50, which includes the best snow in the world! A very good lunch in the business district is about $8. That said, affordability is an issue for the local population, and is critical to the political backdrop—much like it is in the US. This is where it gets interesting. The new Prime Minister recently called for a snap election in an effort to gain more seats in the lower House and strengthen her legislative mandate. If successful, this would allow for more robust implementation of the Prime Minister’s growth policies, which include more accommodative fiscal policy. This led to a spike in JGB yields to start last week at around the same time that the Greenland and European tariff headlines hit markets. records.text: We continue to expect that the BoC will hold its policy rate at 2.25% for all of 2026. While we don’t rule out the possibility that the BoC could normalize policy back towards the middle of its 2.25-3.25% neutral rate range later in the year, we also see (smaller) risks that a renewed downturn in labor market and/or growth data could prompt one or two more cuts to bring the policy rate more squarely into accommodative territory. The main risk, as flagged in our 2026 outlook, is that renewed trade tensions ahead of the USMCA ’s July review deadline could raise upside inflation and downside growth risks for Canada. These concerns have become more pertinent over the last few days, as President Trump has threatened 100% tariffs on Canadian products if Canada moves forward with its recent overtures to strengthen trade relations with China. While we continue to expect only minor changes to the USMCA trade agreement and are not factoring meaningful changes in Canada-US trade policy to our baseline forecast, further escalations would lower the odds of 2026 hikes, in our opinion. As a result, we continue to see hike pricing as somewhat overdone, and our policy rate forecasts are dovish relative to market pricing on both a baseline and risk-adjusted basis (Exhibit 2).
