Scenario 2 – AUD neutral rise in USD FX hedge ratio: Here we illustrate, with simplifying assumptions, how a rise in the USD FX hedge ratio could, in an extreme scenario, be fully offset by a decline in non-USD FX hedge ratios. For the fund included in the article, as of Q3 2025, we estimate 67% of foreign equity holdings were in US equities, equating to AUD63bn of holdings. Should the fund increase its FX hedge ratios on USD equities by 2pp, this would equate to AUD1.3bn of USD selling, we estimate. If this were offset by proportional buying of EUR, JPY and GBP, we think it would equate to AUD0.7bn in EUR buying, AUD0.4bn in JPY buying, and AUD0.2bn in GBP buying. This 2pp rise in the USD FX hedge ratio would therefore equate to a 7pp fall in non- USD FX hedge ratios (see Figure 2). We think this is unrealistic. Figure 2 shows that given the outsized allocation of US equities the fall in non-USD FX hedge ratios required to fully offset any USD selling from rising USD FX hedge ratios would have to be large. In this illustration, USD FX hedge ratios would only be able to rise by 4.6pp in a scenario where non-USD FX hedge ratios were fully reduced to zero. records.text: Inflation stabilised at close to 0% last year, and we expect it to remain subdued but positive throughout this year (Exhibit 3, left). Core inflation should run at around 0.5% in 2026. Towards the end of this year and into 2027 we expect headline inflation to move up towards 0.6%, in line with the SNB’s forecast. A stabilization of inflation at low but positive levels is consistent with inflation and wage expectations (Exhibit 3, right). Short-term inflation expectations have not moved down further since 2025Q2 and firms’ wage growth expectations, at 1.3%, are consistent with inflation around 0.5% and labour productivity growth slightly below 1%. That said, our inflation forecasting framework points to risks to both headline and core inflation being tilted to the downside, particularly if the Swiss Franc remains stronger than we expect and if labour market weakness weighs more strongly on domestic inflation. Therefore, heading into this week’s FOMC meeting, we expect no change in rates or the policy outlook, which remains comfortably on a hold of uncertain duration . In our 2026 Global Outlook , we pencilled in one rate cut for this year (in March) based on the notion that enough weakness would show in the data around the late 2025 government shutdown to provoke one last move lower from Powell. But given the surprising strength of data released in the inter -meeting period, and our above -consensus inflation view, we see a strong possibility that policymakers instead keep rates on hold indefinitely, including after the Fed Chair transition. Our core view is that the FOMC will continue to follow its standing reaction function , despite pressure from the Trump administration. Conceptually, monetary policy is determined by two factors: a country’s economic outlook and a central bank’s policy strategy . While central bank leadership changes have sometimes resulted in material shifts in strategy, the pending transition at the Fed seems unlikely to be one such case, in our view. Severe weather sharply reduced loadings from Novorossiysk and affected Baltic ports, lowering Russian crude exports to 3.1 mbd from 3.7 mbd in December. Despite a sharp drop in exports, Russian crude production declined only modestly by 70-80 kbd to 9.35 mbd in January, while refinery runs fell more sharply to 5.33 mbd. 7. Will shelter inflation fall below 2.75%? Yes. The shelter category is the most important driver statistically of the Phillips curve relationship between inflation and the cyclical state of the economy. In prior cycles, when the economy was at full employment and overall core PCE inflation was at roughly 2%, shelter ran closer to 3% on average. With the “catch-up effect” that kept shelter inflation elevated over the last few years now behind us, and alternative data leading indicators of new lease rent growth now running at just 0.5% year over year, we expect shelter inflation to decline further to 2.3% by the end of this year, a pace that on average would likely have been consistent with below 2% overall core inflation in the past. Our forecast would be a large decline from the current year-over-year pace, which officially stands at 3¼% but is close to 3½% after adjusting for the missing month of shelter inflation last October that will be made up for in April. This should be more than offset by lower capex spending following the decrease in earthquake-related expenditures, which is where we see the bulk of the negative spending impulse coming from. Elevated debt service costs, but stabilising: Debt service costs are arguably the main bugbear for fiscal policy, after rising in both nominal terms and as a share of GDP (3.6% in 2025). A continued need for elevated domestic interest rates while disinflation is sluggish will likely keep debt service costs elevated in 2026. However, we expect these to stabilise as a percentage of GDP as modest rate cuts continue, and if elevated domestic rollover ratios gradually compress, as we expect. Lower rollover ratios: Government plans to reduce the domestic rollover ratio to around 108% in 2026 (the lowest since 2021) from an estimated 133% in 2025, already signal a more cautious and disciplined strategy. In previous years, high rollover ratios reflected a need to refinance large domestic redemptions in a high-inflation environment. The planned decline suggests a move towards further growing the primary surplus, we believe. Primary surpluses to stay in 2026: Türkiye's primary balance closed 2025 with a surplus of around 0.4% of GDP (Figure 1), meaningfully better than the 0.3%-of- GDP deficit forecast in the medium-term programme. A number of countries — including the Antipodes, Scandis, Brazil, Mexico, South Africa, and Chile — have seen outsized currency gains of 4-5% since the start of the year. Initially, tensions around Greenland increased focus on potential de-dollarization flows, and more downbeat US data (e.g., consumer confidence) accelerated the move. Our latest global inflation analysis emphasized the role of currency moves and trade war reverberations in rotating goods price pressures toward the US (and Japan) and away from Europe and Latin America. Input price PMIs are already showing this rotation in response to last year’s dollar slide, and the latest leg lower is likely to strengthen this divide. • In EM, where FX-passthrough tends to be strong and goods account for a larger share of consumer baskets, the dollar’s slide increases policy space both by lowering inflation and reducing financial stability concerns. records.text: e storm begins Total US oil and gas rigs increased by 1 this week to 544, according to Baker Hughes. Oil-focused rigs increased by 1 to 411, after increasing by 1 the previous week. Meanwhile, natural gas- focused rigs remained unchanged at 122, following a decrease of 2 rigs last week. Market attention is now fully focused on the approaching winter storm expected to hit large parts of the US this weekend. Texas has already issued disaster declarations for 134 counties. The storm is expected to be one of the most severe since 2021, with cold conditions likely to persist for at least two days. Snowfall is forecast primarily across northern Texas and the Panhandle. Early production updates are already indicating the emerging impact of the freeze-offs. Current estimates suggest Bakken supply losses of roughly 110–140 kbd, while Anadarko volumes may be down by up to 60 kbd. However, reported daily disruptions do not translate directly into monthly averages, so we assume a more moderate monthly impact, particularly in the Bakken, where we estimate average January losses of around 60 kbd. In the Permian, last year’s milder freeze-offs resulted in approximately 150 kbd of production losses. With temperatures in Midland expected to fall below freezing for up to three days, the risk of a somewhat greater impact this year has increased. Since the December meeting, Swedish inflation has printed below consensus and Riksbank’s expectations, with the sequential momentum in the core inflation series pointing to below-target inflationary pressures over the past months, and the krona has strengthened by around 3%. The Swedish activity picture, meanwhile, remains mixed, with higher-frequency consumer-related indicators pointing to sustained gains in private consumption but the labour market remaining still subdued. We thus expect the Riksbank to stay on hold at 1.75% at their January meeting this week and further ahead. Our probability-weighted path remains below market pricing for a sizeable probability of a hike by the end of this year. MAIN POINTS: 1. At its last meeting in December, the Riksbank’s Executive Board kept the policy rate unchanged at 1.75%, and guided that the “the policy rate is expected to remain at this level for some time to come”. The EU Grids Package, published on 10 December 2025, sets out new rules to accelerate grid deployment and attract investments by streamlining permitting, strengthening EU-level network planning coordination, and granting priority status to t ransmission and distribution infrastructure as an “overriding public interest”. The Commission estimates that around EUR1.2trn of grid spending will be required between now and 2040 (see Key takeaways from the European Grids Package, published by BNP Paribas Equity Research on 11 December 2025). In particular, the package introduced a gap-filling mechanism to expedite the development of cross-border infrastructure, with the aim of achieving an interconnection target of at least 15% by 2030. Under this process, the Commission will identify infrastructure needs and transmission system operators (TSOs) will be given a timeframe to propose projects to meet those needs. If TSOs fail to do that, the gap- filling mechanism will be triggered, allowing third-party developers to step in. We think this could create a sense of urgency among TSOs and keep more project proposals from being outpaced by external developers. What could prevent a muni private credit market from taking shape? • If inflows return to actively managed mutual funds, credit conditions could favor regular-way bond issuance. • A decline in tax receipts could slow infrastructure project planning. • A renewed turndown in commercial real estate could create deal scarcity, as many muni project finance credits have a nexus to land and physical assets. How big could a muni direct lending market become? Over time, we think direct lending could drive up to $30-50bn of annual volume as muni direct lending gradually takes market share from regular bond deals, commercial bank loans, and private placement deals. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 What is direct lending? Defining "private credit 1.0" For us, direct lending means debt extended from a nonbank lender to a municipal or qualified not-for-profit borrower on a bilateral basis. We envisage a market where lenders originate and negotiate terms directly with borrowers, mostly without syndication. Direct loans are not traded on public markets, and are generally valued quarterly. Direct loans also are not publicly rated, though muni loans in a pooled vehicle may eventually receive a credit estimate from a ratings agency. For further reading, see Morgan Stanley Fixed Income Strategists Vishwanath Tirupattur & Joyce Jiang's presentation, Deciphering the Credit in Private Credit. How would muni investors adapt to a direct lending future? Direct lending would be an evolution of muni market structure, not a revolution: • There are over half a dozen interval funds in the market, whose periodic redemption structure allows for a higher allocation to illiquid assets.2 • Pooled securitizations are becoming widely accepted. Though LIHTC housing deals pioneered the structure, deals have also come for other sectors.3 • High yield investors have developed significant expertise in protective covenants, special situations, and debt modifications – all of which would aid direct lending. 2. See New Interval Funds Enter Market, The Bond Buyer, January 22, 2025. 3. See Muni CBOs Step Into High-Yield Market, The Bond Buyer, October 5, 2025.

records.text: The ‘rate check’ by the NY Fed last week, as well as signaling from both the MoF n and BoJ, suggest rising intervention risk in the JPY market. This is in response to ongoing currency and rates volatility, which in turn has been driven by a rise in fundamental inflation risk in the Japanese economy. When rates were at or near the effective lower bound (ELB), it made sense for n real rates to be determined by movements in traded inflation or inflation expectations. This led to — among other things — currency weakness and equity strength as inflation expectations increased. But with JPY traded inflation now approaching target-consistent levels, the n question is whether this dynamic will continue. Evidence from other G3 curves and currencies suggests we could be near a tipping point in currency and rates market correlations, but this will critically depend on domestic policy choices from here. If the policy preference is for intervention rather than tighter monetary or fiscal n policy, relief for Yen and JGBs may be short-lived. In contrast, if intervention is complemented by fiscal restraint, tighter monetary policy and a shift in focus towards upside inflation risks, then it would likely have more durable positive effects on the Yen and JGBs. records.text: odes of sharp bond market and currency movements, the rising volatility in Japanese macro assets over recent years is largely a consequence of the rise in Japanese inflation expectations. With rates at or near the lower bound, and inflation expectations well below target, nominal rates in Japan have been far less volatile than inflation. This means that with nominal rates fixed, or under gradual rate hikes, Japanese real rates have been primarily determined by movements in inflation (Exhibit 2). This means that rising inflation has been a negative for the Yen (and positive for equities) via lower real rates (Exhibit 4). It is also why reports of further fiscal stimulus weaken the Yen rather than strengthen it as standard models would suggest. This is unlike the usual pattern for G10 currencies, where real rates are typically positively correlated with inflation pricing (over longer periods at least), as stronger inflation typically results in higher front-end real rates via the central bank reaction function. Of course, within a liquidity trap or at the policy ELB, and with inflation below target, this is the right policy response to rising inflation expectations. The post -FOMC data will mostly sharpen analysts ’ forecasts for Q4 GDP. Thursday’s international trade balance ( -$44.0bn vs. -$29.4bn) will be the focus on this front given the volatility in the recent trade data. However, Fed officials are more likely to focus on Thursday’s jobless claims (215k vs. 200k) and Friday’s December PPI (+0.3% headline / +0.3% core) to inform their near -term outlooks for the labor market and inflation. Regarding the former, we expect some payback from depressed claims during the holiday week. records.text: M Idea 4 Supply – When a Loan Works Better than a Bond HY muni mutual funds’ need for bonds, not loans, creates structural inefficiencies that add to financing costs. Said differently, sometimes we think a loan would be a superior solution for a project finance credit. First, underwriting costs for HY deals can be steep. Just as traditional private credit serves the middle market, most muni HY borrowers are smaller. Since many issuance costs are fixed regardless of par size (attorneys' fees, servicing fees, trustee fees), smaller bond deals are inherently inefficient. Second, and crucially, covenant violations are more costly for bonds than for loans. In the bond context, covenant violations trigger timely and expensive reporting obligations. Hypothetically, covenants can be waived quickly. In practice, however, investors may not be unanimous, creating a collective action problem. This collective action problem makes workouts even more costly. None of this is ideal for investors, either: • Muni traders easily misconstrue covenant violations, often driving price declines that overshoot fair value. • By contrast, a loan offers a more streamlined approach to managing speculative credits. Loan modifications are a bilateral negotiation. Simple disclosure events can be addressed without driving unnecessary price volatility. records.text: While KRW hedging demand from foreign equity holdings will remain relevant, its depreciation pressure on the KRW should diminish over time due to its inherently countercyclical nature and the nearly 80% equity market gain since mid-2025. A persistent KRW depreciation—if sustained by uncorrected structural FX imbalances or risk-off shocks—would benefit Korea’s major export sectors (tech, shipbuilding, autos), which account for 50% of exports and 57% of equity market cap (Exhibit 8). Our input output analysis suggests that a 10% KRW depreciation raises overall manufacturing margins by 2 percentage points, with roughly double the impact in the tech sector which already benefits greatly from strong AI-demand. If KRW levels remain disconnected from fundamentals despite rising exporter profitability and stronger activity, appreciation pressures would continue to accumulate over the medium term through larger trade surpluses, improved export competitiveness, and renewed foreign portfolio inflows. Moreover, persistent KRW weakness at current levels could lift corporate tax revenues by about 0.5% of GDP per our estimation, allowing for targeted fiscal support for domestic industries hit by continued KRW depreciation. records.text: AI to measure what central banks say . Using Large Language Models (LLM), we analyse policy-relevant remarks in speeches, interviews and press conferences and score them on a hawkish/dovish scale. We show what topics and speakers are driving the shifts in sentiment and provide narrative maps and timelines to illustrate how institutional language evolves. Updated daily, the dataset spans over two decades and is accessible via an interactive dashboard and a Python API ( >Access Dataset ). ECB communication has moved back towards neutral after a dovish phase in Q4. This adjustment is being mostly driven by growth-related language, which remains the marginal swing factor in the ECB's tone, while the inflation tone has been broadly stable since the summer of 2025, closely tracking the underlying data and contributing little to the recent shift in overall sentiment. Evidence from early 2026 is limited but consistent with this picture: Philip Lane has returned to more hawkish language while Luis de Guindos has remained mildly dovish, in line with his historical positioning. See page 2/3 for detail. This report has been prepared by UBS AG London Branch. records.text: 10 Questions for 2026 In this US Economics Analyst, we present our top 10 questions for the coming year. 1. Will GDP growth beat consensus expectations? Yes. Our forecast for 2026 Q4/Q4 GDP growth is 2.5%, above consensus at 2.1% for the fourth year in a row. On a full-year basis, our forecast is 2.9% vs. 2.4% consensus. Exhibit 1 shows that we are above consensus on most components of GDP . We are furthest above consensus on business investment (discussed below) and furthest below on net exports, in both cases partly because we expect substantial further growth of investment in imported equipment for AI. Despite being well above consensus, we do not see our GDP forecast as boldly optimistic and in fact see some risk of even higher growth this year. After all, 2025 Q4/Q4 GDP growth is tracking at around 2.5%, the mechanical effect of the last government shutdown on Q4/Q4 growth will swing from roughly -0.3pp in 2025 to +0.3pp in 2026, and the sum of the growth impulses that we estimate from changes in government policy and financial conditions shown in Exhibit 2 swings from -0.2pp to +0.3pp. Our forecast is a bit more conservative than this math might imply because we think the economy’s potential growth rate of a bit over 2% is a better launching-off point than last year’s growth rate, especially in light of the distortions to the GDP numbers caused by frontloading ahead of tariffs and mismeasurement. Across major markets, grid modernization has moved to the forefront of policy agendas, supported by regulatory reform and multi-year capex commitments . We think this should create durable growth visibility for companies across the grid infrastructure and energy storage supply chain. Defensive nature: We like the theme’s defensive characteristics. A significant portion of transmission and distribution assets operate under regulatory regimes, delivering stable and predictable revenue streams over extended horizons. records.text: The Korean won (KRW) weakened again in January, reversing its sharp rebound in late December. This occurred despite a strong KOSPI rally, with Korea’s equity market up 18% year‑to‑date and outperforming regional peers. By mid‑January, the KRW had returned to elevated early‑December levels even as most Asian currencies strengthened or remained broadly stable (Exhibit 1). This divergence—KRW weakness alongside robust equity performance—marks a notable departure from the KRW’s usual procyclical behavior and its long‑standing positive correlation with risk assets. KRW Drivers The recent appearance of the KRW’s counter‑cyclicality does not seem to have originated in spot markets. Two key spot‑market drivers—total outbound retail investment and foreign equity outflows—declined by half in January (Exhibit 2). Foreign equity flows turned positive for the first three weeks of January from overall net outflows in Q4. Retail outflows appear to have moderated partly in response to stabilization measures introduced in December, including tax incentives for domestic or hedged foreign investments and strengthened prudential rules aimed at creating a more even competitive environment between onshore and offshore products. records.text: The pace and sourcing of US power infrastructure is a front and center area of focus for investors given implications for the pace of AI deployment as a driver of our 2.6% CAGR in US power demand through 2030. In this note, we analyze the generation capacity data from the EIA to track currently planned and added capacity. We believe Parts/People availability are among the key drivers/constraints to AI/data center (and broader) power demand growth, and the latest EIA data is supportive for renewables development through 2030 amid policy incentives sunsetting. We provide further details regarding net generation additions by technology and color on planned projects, such as cumulative delays and cancellations. Capacity additions totaled ~50 GW in 2025, making up 80% of our estimates for 2025. December additions lagged in 2025, with only 19% of the YTD capacity added that month compared to an average of 38% of yearly capacity being added in the last month of the year since 2017. By technology, wind capacity additions and coal retirements were roughly in-line with our expectations in 2025, while storage and CCGT surpassed our estimates at 122% and 165% of GSe. The main laggards were simple cycle gas and solar additions, reaching only 53% and 74% of GSe in 2025, respectively, even though nominally, solar capacity adds were strong at 29 GW making up for 57% of total yearly additions. We initiated a paid position in Feb/May RBA ahead of the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) December 2025 meeting, citing the risk of a more hawkish stance due to upside surprises in inflation (see AUD rates: Pay Feb/May RBA spread, dated 5 December 2025). The central bank did adopt a more hawkish tone at its December meeting as we had expected, ruling out rate cuts and warning of potential rate hikes if inflation momentum proved more persistent than expected. Since then, front-end AUD rates have exhibited asymmetric pricing behavior, with a greater tendency to price in additional hikes on strong data, while responding more mutedly to weak data, and the spread has widened over time (Figure 2). Q4 CPI print decides Feb RBA: With the Q4 CPI release scheduled for this Wednesday (28 Jan), markets are expecting a 0.9% q/q print in the trimmed mean, exceeding the RBA's November forecast of 0.8% q/q. However, economist estimates vary widely, ranging from 0.7% to 1.0%. As a result, Feb RBA remains only 60% priced, at 15bp. Currently, market consensus seems to be that the RBA will hold if the print comes in at 0.8% q/q, but will hike if it reaches 0.9% q/q. KEY MESSAGES We expect Türkiye to maintain fiscal discipline and implement measured rate cuts in H1, which should support Turkish government bonds. Tax revenue should remain buoyant, given our expectation for resilient growth of 3.8% in 2026. We maintain the TRY and duration overweights in our model portfolio. We think the belly of the curve is starting to look more attractive than the front end for duration returns. This is not yet true for front-end real rates, which although off the lows, are still deeply negative. Moreover, the market is still trading as if real rates will stay low and policy will stay behind the curve, with stronger inflation or expansionary fiscal policy resulting in a weaker currency and steeper curves. But we should be on the lookout for further signs of change in trading patterns towards the G10 norm — and, as we discuss below, any policy changes that would warrant this shift. One relationship worth watching is the correlation between the level of 2y JGB yields and the 2s10s curve slope. Over the last 30 years, consistent with being near the ELB, any movement higher in 2y yields has corresponded with a steeper 2s10s curve (Exhibit 5). But if we narrow the sample to periods where 2y yields were above 1%, we find that the 2s10s curve typically traded with a low or even negative correlation to front-end rates (Exhibit 6). Current 2y yields are 1.2%, suggesting the risks are skewed towards a flatter curve should 2y rates rise from here — again, this correlation pattern would be the G10 norm. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 What Deal Structuring Could Look Like Make fuller use of capital structure A muni private credit fund would be better positioned to maximize value across the entire capital structure. Lack of equity is a challenge for traditional muni project finance credit. Direct lending could have more freedom and flexibility in this regard. Of course, governmental credits may not be in a position to sell equity, as their underlying assets are publicly owned. Still, even governmental projects can benefit from equity-like subordinated tranches. They figure in a number of HY student and senior housing transactions. The subordinated opportunity set is also not limited to smaller borrowers. Puerto Rico’s landmark emergence from bankruptcy was aided by a contingent value instrument – an equity-like note whose payouts are tied to surplus growth in governmental funds. Of course, subordinated and contingent value instruments are all possible in a public markets context. In practice, however, most HY investors prefer a senior tranche, as subordinated and contingent notes are often taxable. records.text: In an environment where productivity growth has rebounded to 2% this cycle, as shown in Exhibit 10, this 3.5% pace of wage growth is likely compatible with inflation below 2%. While inflation in labor-intensive core services categories is still a bit higher than would typically be consistent with 2% overall inflation, it is likely to continue to catch down to the rate implied by softer wage pressures. This softer starting point for the labor market is the key reason that we do not share the recent concern of some investors that fiscal expansion in the US and other advanced economies could stoke a revival of inflationary pressures this year. While it is directionally reasonable to expect above-trend growth supported by fiscal stimulus to tighten the labor market and increase wage and price pressures, the effect should be modest from the current starting point and partly offset by other headwinds to hiring. 6. Will core goods inflation fall at least 1pp? Yes. Core PCE inflation likely ended 2025 in roughly the same place as it began, but this stability was the product of two offsetting forces: a continued decline in the underlying inflation trend visible in core services categories coupled with a bump from tariff effects mainly in goods categories. Exhibit 11 shows that the tariff bump has raised core goods inflation to a pace roughly 2pp above its pre-pandemic rate. records.text: European bond supply is another reason to expect the EUR curve to remain steep. Persistently higher borrowing needs, especially for Germany and the EU, should maintain a steep long end, particularly given the relatively slow pace of WAM reduction in Europe vs, say, the UK or Japan. In our macro model, each percentage point of free float (the debt stock less central bank holdings) usually steepens 10s30s by about 1bp. However, in the current duration demand environment and with a high hurdle to adjust ECB QT we think markets will be more sensitive than usual to long-end issuance, and a further easing of Bund scarcity is likely to raise that sensitivity, at least for bonds. That said, signals so far this year suggest bond supply absorption is going smoothly, with strong demand at syndications – as evidenced by bid-to-cover ratios – even as volume issued reached new highs and syndications included 20y bonds in France and Italy (Exhibit 7). Stability in Bund spreads also suggests good absorption in the core. records.text: ructure of Medicare Advantage. As Medicare Part C, it is a form of Medicare coverage administered by private insurance companies rather than by the government’s traditional fee for service program. Private insurers take responsibility for managing enrollee care. In return, they receive capitation payments from the government. These payments are central to the revenues that insurers record in their financial statements. The link to inflation arises because both CPI and PCE measure health insurance inflation using data on insurer premium revenues, rather than directly tracking consumer paid premiums. When Medicare Advantage payments come in weaker than expected, insurers’ premium revenues also weaken, and this causes lower measured health insurance inflation. In the case of CPI, the impact is especially delayed and soft. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) uses an indirect method that relies on the National Association of Insurance Commissioners' (NAIC) financial statements. Health insurance CPI inflation is calculated using a two year moving average of retained earnings ratios, defined as the ratio between earnings (earned premiums minus medical expenses) and medical expenses. If Medicare Advantage payments decline relative to expectations and insurers do not offset the revenue loss with efficiency gains that reduce medical expenses, then retained earnings in 2027 will fall. Prior to the start of the RBA’s hiking cycle in 2002 and 2009, the correlation was weak, but re-established itself just before the first cut. records.text: Capacity Additions Tracker: 50 GW of operating capacity added in 2025 Net generation capacity additions to the system totaled ~50 GW in 2025, with utility scale solar and battery net additions of 29 GW and 16 GW YTD, respectively (Exhibit 1). Total net additions fell short of our expectations in 2025, making up 80% of our total net capacity addition estimates of 63 GW for 2025 (65% in November). Notably, storage, wind and CCGT additions ended the year surpassing or meeting our expectations at 122%, 98% and 165% of our full year capacity addition estimates, while simple cycle gas and solar fell short, reaching only 53% and 74% of our 2025 estimates. Finally, ~5GW of net coal capacity was retired in 2025 compared to our expectation of ~5.5GW, marking 91% of our 2025 expectation. We believe less coal retirements could be a short-term solution to meet increasing power demand and offset potentially slower capacity additions from other technologies. Meanwhile, indicators of activity came in stronger than anticipated, with GDP growth for Q3 printing 4.4% q/q saar and private domestic final purchases rising 2.9% q/q saar, led by a robust 3.5% q/q saar increase in consumer spending. Real consumer spending continued to grow at a similar pace in October and November, though these estimates are likely exaggerated by downward biases in inflation estimates, due to shutdown-related distortions. In any case, consumer spending appears to be running well ahead of income. Inflation has generally surprised to the downside, with core PCE inflation rounding to 0.2% m/m in October and November. Both months saw core goods prices flatten, while core services prices firmed. We view much of the softness as reflecting distortions related to the government shutdown. Looking ahead, we expect monthly inflation prints to firm notably, likely through April 2026, as the downward biases from October and November get reversed, and tariffs- related cost increases get passed onto consumer prices. We estimate core PCE inflation rose 0.45% m/m increase in December. In all, we think core PCE inflation came in at 2.9% Q4/Q4 in 2025 and will be little changed, at 2.8% Q4/Q4, in 2026. Meanwhile, survey-based measures of inflation expectations remain at historically elevated levels, with measures from the Conference Board, and the NY Fed consumer expectations having moved largely sideways over the past few months. The University of Michigan's measure, on the other hand, shows some easing at the margin for January 2026. For the longer run, the University of Michigan measure of 5-10y ahead expectations rose by 0.1pp to 3.3% in the preliminary January reading (Figure 11), while the New York Fed measures of inflation expectations three and five years ahead were little changed for December, the latest reading, at 3.0%. We think the ramifications of missing October prices and limited sampling in November are likely to be felt in January and again in April 2026, biasing the inflation estimates higher. In addition, we continue to expect tariff pass-through to prop up core goods prices materially in Q1 26. In all, we forecast core PCE inflation at 2.9% Q4/Q4 in 2025, about one-tenth lower than the median forecast in the December SEP , and easing to 2.8% Q4/Q4 in 2026, 0.3pp higher than in the December SEP . 26 January 2026 8 Barclays | Federal Reserve Commentary

records.text: M Idea 2 Focus on the risks Bottom line | Unchanged rates: We expect the Riksbank to remain on hold at the January meeting and reiterate that the policy rate will remain at the current level for the foreseeable future. The policy rate path from December sent a clear signal that the Board expects no rate change at least for the upcoming three quarters. Since the meeting, the December inflation print surprised to the downside (by 29bp on core inflation) and the SEK has strengthened more than anticipated (Exhibit 3 ). We would expect the Riksbank to acknowledge the lower inflation print and flag the risk of weaker inflationary pressures, both posing a downside risk to the December inflation projections. Given that Sweden was included amongst the countries facing the potential additional 10% US tariffs connected to Greenland, we would expect the press release to also focus on the associated heightened uncertainty and possible adverse growth implications. Balance of risks: The minutes from the December meeting also shed light on the balance of risks. Half the Board sees forward looking indicators having a bias towards downside risks to inflation (Jansson, Bunge). And while there is a potential for upside pressures to inflation outlook, they are not materializing (Seim). The stronger growth seen in the Swedish economy is also a welcome development and not an inflationary concern, as high spare capacity limits the risk of demand driven inflationary pressures (Bunge, Thedeen). Third, a lower tax on electricity from January 2026 (a reduction of 9.875 öre per kWh including VAT) is being introduced as part of the 2026 Budget, and we estimate -20bp impact on CPIF from this reduction. We therefore expect CPIF ex energy declining to 2.0%Y and CPIF to 1.8%Y in January 2026.
